title: Ezra 3:1–13
context: After the return under Cyrus and the list of those who came up (Ezra 1–2), the returned community gathers at Jerusalem in the seventh month, the month of the trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the feast of booths (Leviticus 23:23–43). The narrative gives no year for this gathering; many readers take it to be the first year of the return, since 3:8 counts from their coming. Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel rebuild the altar on its base and restore the offerings written in the law of Moses, even though the temple’s foundation is not yet laid (3:1–6). Materials are arranged in a way that recalls Solomon’s preparations (3:7; compare 1 Kings 5:6–9 and 2 Chronicles 2:16), and in the second year the work begins under Levitical oversight (3:8–9). When the foundation is laid, priests and Levites praise the LORD according to David’s order with the refrain heard at the dedication of Solomon’s temple (2 Chronicles 5:13; 7:3); many shout for joy while the old men who had seen the first house weep, and the two sounds cannot be told apart (3:10–13). Parallels and related notices, named without harmonization: Ezra calls Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, while 1 Chronicles 3:17–19 lists him among the sons of Pedaiah, Shealtiel’s brother; Nehemiah 7:73–8:1 uses closely similar wording about the seventh month and the people gathering as one man, but there the gathering is to hear Ezra read the law; Ezra 5:16 credits Sheshbazzar with laying the foundations of God’s house, while this chapter narrates the foundation under Zerubbabel and Jeshua; and Haggai 2:18 and Zechariah 4:9 speak of the foundation being laid in the days of Darius. Readers propose different ways of relating these notices, and this commentary does not settle them. The mingled joy and weeping is shared ground for both traditions: honest worship before a faithful God who is restoring his people from small beginnings.

verses.text: When the seventh month had come, and the children of Israel were in the cities, the people gathered themselves together as one man to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice that the people gather as one man, a community acting together in response to the LORD who has brought them home. The seventh month was rich with appointed worship (Leviticus 23:23–43), and the returned exiles choose to begin there, showing a willing and united response to grace already received in the return itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers connect this gathering with the stirring of God mentioned at Ezra 1:1 and 1:5, where the LORD moved Cyrus and moved the households who went up. Shared ground: both traditions see a restored people rightly turning first to worship, and both read their unity as a gift of God that also calls for real, wholehearted human participation.

verses.text: Then Jeshua the son of Jozadak stood up with his brothers the priests and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and his relatives, and built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the law of Moses the man of God.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel, the leader of David’s line, build the altar together, which Arminian readers see as covenant obedience shared by priest and people. They rebuild according to what is written in the law of Moses, not by invention, and their first act is to restore the offerings by which Israel drew near to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that worship is regulated by what God has written, so the altar is rebuilt as it is written in the law of Moses. Shared ground: both traditions read these sacrifices, with Hebrews 10:1, as part of a law that was a shadow of good things to come, and both see the restored altar as God’s appointed way of approach for that day. Jeshua appears in Haggai 1:1 as Joshua the son of Jehozadak.

verses.text: In spite of their fear because of the peoples of the surrounding lands, they set the altar on its base; and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, even burnt offerings morning and evening.
verses.arminianNotes: The returned community sets the altar on its base in spite of their fear of the surrounding peoples. Arminian readers note that faith here is not the absence of fear but obedience chosen under pressure, and that the morning and evening burnt offerings (compare Exodus 29:38–39) express a daily, renewed dependence on the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the people casting themselves on God’s protection rather than on their own strength, since they have no walls, no temple, and powerful neighbors. Shared ground: both traditions read the daily offerings as a confession that the community’s security rests on the LORD, and both note that the fear named here prepares the reader for the open opposition of chapter 4.

verses.text: They kept the feast of booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number, according to the ordinance, as the duty of every day required;
verses.arminianNotes: They keep the feast of booths as it is written and offer the daily burnt offerings by number, following the pattern of Numbers 29:12–38. Arminian readers note that the feast recalled the wilderness, when Israel lived in temporary shelters (Leviticus 23:42–43), a fitting memory for exiles newly returned and still unsettled, who now respond with careful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the feast a remembrance that the LORD alone sustained Israel in the wilderness and has now sustained them in exile and return. Shared ground: both traditions read the careful observance as a recovery of covenant worship after the loss of the land, and both see the same faithful God at work in the exodus and in this second coming out.

verses.text: and afterward the continual burnt offering, the offerings of the new moons, of all the set feasts of the LORD that were consecrated, and of everyone who willingly offered a free will offering to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Alongside the continual offering, the new moons, and the set feasts comes everyone who willingly offered a free will offering, echoing the free will gifts of Ezra 2:68. Arminian readers value this voluntary devotion as a real response of grateful hearts, offered freely beyond what the law required of the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the free will offerings as fruit of God’s work in his people, who give willingly because he has made them willing, while also honoring what the law commanded (compare Numbers 29:39). Shared ground: both traditions hold together required worship and glad, voluntary giving, and neither treats the willing gift as mere duty or as a means of earning favor.

verses.text: From the first day of the seventh month, they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD; but the foundation of the LORD’s temple was not yet laid.
verses.arminianNotes: From the first day of the seventh month the offerings resume, though the foundation of the temple is not yet laid. Arminian readers note that the people do what is within reach now rather than waiting for ideal conditions, offering faithful worship at an altar under the open sky while the larger work still lies ahead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see here that the LORD may be truly worshiped by his appointed means even before the house is rebuilt, since his presence is not bound to a building. Shared ground: both traditions read the order of the chapter, altar before foundation, as putting worship first, and both see the unfinished temple as a reminder that restoration is begun and not yet complete.

verses.text: They also gave money to the masons and to the carpenters. They also gave food, drink, and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa, according to the grant that they had from Cyrus King of Persia.
verses.arminianNotes: Money for masons and carpenters, and food, drink, and oil for the people of Sidon and Tyre, bring cedar from Lebanon to Joppa, much as in Solomon’s day (1 Kings 5:6–9; 2 Chronicles 2:16). Arminian readers value this planning, labor, and trade as genuine human participation in God’s work, carried out through ordinary skills and agreements.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the work proceeds according to the grant from Cyrus, a pagan king whose decree the LORD himself prompted (Ezra 1:1–4), illustrating that the king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand (Proverbs 21:1). Shared ground: both traditions see divine provision working through rulers, commerce, and skilled labor, and both hear in the echo of Solomon a sign of continuity with the first house.

verses.text: Now in the second year of their coming to God’s house at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the rest of their brothers the priests and the Levites, and all those who had come out of the captivity to Jerusalem, began the work and appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to have the oversight of the work of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: In the second year, in the second month, the leaders and all who had come out of the captivity begin the work, appointing Levites from twenty years old and upward as in David’s arrangement (1 Chronicles 23:24, 27). Arminian readers note the shared effort of leaders and people, and many readers observe that Solomon also began in the second month (1 Kings 6:1; 2 Chronicles 3:2), though the text does not comment on the match.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see continuity of God’s ordered worship from David to the restoration, with the Levites again serving under an arrangement God had established among his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the careful organization as faithfulness, not bureaucracy, and both see the whole community, not only its leaders, joined in beginning the work of the LORD’s house.

verses.text: Then Jeshua stood with his sons and his brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together to have the oversight of the workmen in God’s house: the sons of Henadad, with their sons and their brothers the Levites.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeshua with his sons and brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, and the sons of Henadad oversee the workmen. Arminian readers note that names like Jeshua and Kadmiel also appear among the returning Levites in Ezra 2:40, and they value how Scripture records ordinary servants by name, honoring faithful labor that most histories would leave anonymous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see these overseers as people God placed in their callings, each family serving in its appointed role so that the work is done decently and in order. Shared ground: both traditions read the list as dignifying ordinary vocations in God’s service, and both see that the rebuilding depends on many hands rather than on a single hero.

verses.text: When the builders laid the foundation of the LORD’s temple, they set the priests in their vestments with trumpets, with the Levites the sons of Asaph with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: When the builders lay the foundation, priests with trumpets and Levites of the sons of Asaph with cymbals praise the LORD according to the directions of David (compare 1 Chronicles 16:4–6 and 25:1). Arminian readers note that the community answers God’s faithfulness with ordered, public, and joyful praise, gladly taking up the worship David had arranged.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see worship again conformed to an ordering that Scripture traces back to David, so that the restored community stands in continuity with the worship of the first temple. Shared ground: both traditions read the musical service as fitting praise for God’s faithfulness, and both see the foundation laying as a moment to confess what God has done before celebrating what the builders have done.

verses.text: They sang to one another in praising and giving thanks to the LORD, “For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever toward Israel.” All the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the LORD’s house had been laid.
verses.arminianNotes: The people sing to one another the refrain heard at the dedication of Solomon’s temple (2 Chronicles 5:13; 7:3; compare Psalm 136), here with the added words toward Israel, and all the people shout. Arminian readers stress that God’s loving kindness is experienced again by a people who had known judgment, and that it invites a glad and wholehearted response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in the refrain God’s enduring covenant love, which did not fail through exile and which is the ground of Israel’s restoration. Shared ground: both traditions read this song as the heart of the chapter: the LORD is good, his loving kindness endures, and the great shout of the people is a fitting answer to his faithfulness.

verses.text: But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers’ households, the old men who had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice. Many also shouted aloud for joy,
verses.arminianNotes: Many of the priests, Levites, and heads of households, the old men who had seen the first house, weep with a loud voice while many shout for joy. The text does not explain the weeping; Arminian readers often connect it with Haggai 2:3, where the prophet asks who remembers the former glory, and see honest grief brought before God alongside praise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the tears as grief over what was lost, which may include sorrow over the judgment that destroyed the first house, though the text does not say so directly. Shared ground: both traditions refuse to rank the two responses here, since the narrative records weeping and joy side by side, and both hear an echo of Zechariah 4:10 on not despising the day of small things.

verses.text: so that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people; for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard far away.
verses.arminianNotes: The noise of the shout of joy cannot be distinguished from the noise of weeping, and it is heard far away. Arminian readers see a picture of real worship that holds memory and hope together, where a people neither denies its losses nor withholds its thanks, and freely brings both before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the mingled sound a people living between judgment and full restoration, sustained by God’s faithfulness in both. Shared ground: both traditions read the blended shout and weeping as an honest response of faith, and many readers note that the sound heard far away prepares for 4:1, where the adversaries hear of the building.
